title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
author: Heather Cherone
content:
Chicago's finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses,
spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and
financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial
decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess.

The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding
hard choices for expediency leads to trouble.

The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its
corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its
pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be
repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to
ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money
to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at
its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate
fund.

Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years
that dug the city into such a massive financial hole.

### Pension Holiday Snowballs Into Peril

In 2000, the city’s pensions were 85% funded, which meant the funds could
easily pay benefits to employees as they retired, records show. But a series
of decisions in both Chicago and the Illinois capital of Springfield unraveled
that strong position, leading to the current mountain of $36.4 billion in
pension debt.

First, the twin blows of the “dot-com” bubble bursting in 2000 and the Great
Recession in 2007 wiped out nearly $16 billion from those funds.

Around the same time came a self-inflicted blow. In 2005, the state
legislature, at the request of then Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, passed
legislation allowing the city to contribute less every year than what was
actually needed to pay retirees.

As a result, in 2006 and 2007, Daley was able to stop making annual
contributions to four pension funds for police officers, firefighters,
laborers and municipal employees. He received near-unanimous support from the
Chicago City Council. Daley, who was mayor from 1989 through 2011, declined to
comment for this story.

![A close-up photo of a man in a suit gesturing with this
hand.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/AP060809022266_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)Former
Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley in 2006 Julio Cortez/AP

Daley’s “pension holiday” meant the city could balance its budget without a
politically perilous property tax hike. But that maneuver laid the foundation
of the current pension crisis facing the city.  

In 2010, having seen the financial fallout from the pension legislation, state
legislators passed a law that banned city officials from taking another
pension holiday by setting a firm schedule for the city to pay back its
skipped payments — no excuses allowed.

Two of Chicago’s pension funds must be funded at a 90% level by 2055, with the
other two hitting that mark by 2058, according to state law. This requirement
caused a spike in the city’s annual payments.

Trying to ease Chicago’s snowballing pension burdens, lawmakers passed a new
measure reducing the retirement benefits offered to state employees who began
work on or after January 1, 2011.

But that revised law touched off a new set of problems. The well-intentioned
effort to reduce costs actually reduced pension benefits too drastically.
Under federal law, public sector pension funds must pay workers no less than
what they would have earned if they paid into Social Security.

In 2021 and 2025, lawmakers agreed to change the law and ensure that first
responders — police and firefighters — in Illinois are paid at least the
minimum required by law.

Fixing those funds will cost Chicago an additional $11 billion to get to the
90% funded level required by state law over the next three decades, according
to city projections. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the legislation over the
objections of city officials.

### Long-Term Lease, Long-Lasting Regrets

Facing big deficits in 2008 in the wake of the Great Recession, Daley and the
City Council found what they thought was a creative solution to the city’s
financial woes.

They would lease the city’s parking meters to a conglomerate of investment
funds for 75 years in return for $1.5 billion up front. That massive influx of
cash meant no one had to make any hard decisions to fill the city’s budget gap
and avoid a politically unpopular property tax increase.

![A man in business attire presses buttons on a parking meter on a city
street.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/AP090528042311_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)A
Chicago resident feeds a new parking meter in 2009. The city privatized its
parking meters in a $1.1 billion, 75-year deal as a way to get a cash
infusion. Charles Rex Arbogast/AP

But the deal ended up a loser both politically and financially.

The new owners of the meters immediately jacked up the cost to park,
infuriating residents. In a matter of months, members of the City Council
began regretting their votes, and Daley announced he would not run for
reelection.

By 2025, the city’s meters generated $2.2 billion in revenue for the
investors, with another 58 years still left on the lease.

The city considered buying the parking meters back this year, but Mayor
Brandon Johnson told reporters “the final purchase price was far too high.”
The city would have had to borrow billions to finance the $3.2 billion
purchase.

Elected officials across the political spectrum agree that the city would have
been much better off raising property taxes instead of leasing the parking
meters in 2008.

But even as the gap between the city’s revenues and its expenses continues to
widen, property tax hikes remain the third rail of Chicago politics.

Chicagoans’ property taxes last jumped in 2021, when former Mayor Lori
Lightfoot raised them by $93.9 million and passed a budget that automatically
hiked property taxes to keep pace with inflation.

Johnson campaigned against those automatic property tax increases, forcing
Lightfoot to drop a proposal to hike taxes by $42.7 million in 2023, just
months before she lost her bid for reelection.

The automatic property tax hike was eliminated, even though it could have
prevented the city’s credit rating from being downgraded repeatedly and
significantly reduced the annual budget gaps.

In a postscript to the parking meter debacle, Chicago Parking Meters LLC sold
the meters contract earlier this year to an investment firm, triggering a one-
time payment to the city of $75 million. The City Council and Johnson then
battled over how best to use that money for pension costs, creating a
temporary hole in the 2027 city budget.

### The Financial Toll of Police Misconduct

The 2014 police murder of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald changed nearly every
aspect of City Hall politics around policing. Despite decades of scandals,
misconduct and brutality, the Police Department had managed to fend off
reform. But that ended with McDonald’s death, even as city leaders continued
to fear a backlash from residents concerned about crime rates and a
politically powerful police union.

After a massive outcry greeted footage of McDonald getting shot 16 times while
he walked away from officers, the federal government launched a probe that in
2017 found ample evidence that the department ​​routinely violated the
constitutional rights of Black and Latino Chicagoans.

![A crowd of people embrace outside a government building. Some of the people
are in tears. One person holds a protest sign that says, “Justice for Laquan …
convict Van Dyke.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/AP18278849071586_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)People
react outside of City Hall in 2018 after a jury convicted former Chicago
police Officer Jason Van Dyke of second-degree murder in the 2014 shooting of
teenager Laquan McDonald. Matt Marton/AP

In 2019, the Chicago Police Department agreed — under the oversight of a
federal judge — to change the way officers are trained, supervised and
disciplined. In taking so long to address a pernicious problem, a succession
of city leaders set up Chicago for a huge financial hit.

The true scope of police misconduct and what it will cost the city is only now
becoming clear.

From 2019 to 2025, as the city scrambled to fill budget holes, it agreed to
pay nearly $730 million to resolve lawsuits alleging officers committed a wide
range of misconduct, according to a WTTW News analysis of city records. The
most expensive cases involve wrongful convictions that sent Chicagoans now
declared innocent to prison for decades, as well as botched raids and police
pursuits that violated CPD policy and led to injuries, according to that
analysis.

In 2026 alone, Chicago has spent more than $277 million to resolve lawsuits
alleging police misconduct, records show. That includes nearly $100 million to
resolve 90 lawsuits filed by people who allege they were wrongfully implicated
based on evidence gathered by former Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was convicted in
2013 of taking bribes. He has denied wrongdoing.

Johnson has urged the City Council to borrow an additional $481 million to
cover the costs of resolving more lawsuits, with $260.8 million earmarked for
17 people wrongfully convicted based on evidence developed by former Chicago
police Detective Reynaldo Guevara. A judge determined Guevara told “bald-faced
lies” while under oath in 2017, a fact that will be presented to any jury
asked to determine whether the city should be held accountable for claims of
misconduct. He has repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right not to
incriminate himself when pressed to testify in civil cases.

Another 25 lawsuits naming Guevara remain pending.

Guevara is now one of the most notorious members of the Chicago Police
Department, costing taxpayers more than any other officer, including former
Cmdr. Jon Burge, who tortured and beat more than 100 Black men from the 1970s
to the 1990s, city officials have acknowledged.

Records show that Guevara, who retired from CPD in 2005 and lives in Texas,
collects an annual payout of $91,000 from the city’s depleted police pension
fund.
